Minimizes side-effects of high-dose treatments.

title: Glycan Age Prediction Model
meta_description: Researchers at the University of California, Davis, have developed a model to estimate biological and chronological age from blood serum samples.
summary: Researchers at the University of California, Davis, have developed a model to estimate biological and chronological age from blood serum samples.
description:
Alterations in the human glycome have been associated with cancer and autoimmunity. Thus, constructing a site-specific map of the human glycome for biomarker research and discovery has been a highly sought-after objective. However, due to analytical barriers, comprehensive site-specific glycoprofiling is difficult to perform.

Researchers at the University of California, Davis have developed a platform to detect easily quantifiable, site-specific, disease-associated glycan alterations for clinical applications by adapting the Multiple Reaction Monitoring (MRM) Mass Spectrometry (MS) method for use in glycan biomarker research. The adaptations allow for highly precise site-specific glycan monitoring with minimum sample preparation. MRM MS was employed to construct a detailed, site-specific structural map of the human plasma glycome of healthy individuals and to characterize the glycans’ inter- and intra-molecular correlations. Glycan alterations associated with age and gender (common covariants in biomarker research and discovery) were also identified and multi-analyte classifiers capable of predicting age were constructed and validated.
applications:
-
Glycan biomarker research and discovery.
-
Development of novel glycan-altering therapeutics.
advantages:
-
Characterize the human glycome in a rapid and reproducible fashion.
-
Detects quantifiable, site-specific, disease-associated glycan alterations more efficiently than previous glycan age prediction models.

title: Algorithmic Lifestyle Optimization in Personalized Medicine
meta_description: Researchers at the University of California, Davis have developed an algorithm that uses data from group testing to rapidly provide lifestyle optimizations that improve the health of patients.
summary:
Researchers at the University of California, Davis have
developed an algorithm that uses data from group testing to rapidly provide
lifestyle optimizations that improve the health of patients.
description:
Personalized medicine is a growing
industry where treatment options are customized based on an individual’s
specific physiology and medical history. This approach shows particularly
promising results in the treatment of chronic medical conditions using
personalized diet and exercise recommendations. To make such recommendations, biomarkers
are commonly taken through blood or urine samples and analyzed. However, the
predictive power of these biomarkers is typically unreliable, resulting in
inconclusive treatment recommendations. A more reliable method of personalized
medicine is the standard elimination approach, where variables are introduced
one at a time to see their immediate impact on an individual’s health. While the standard elimination method is more
precise, it takes much longer to isolate many compounding variables. For
instance, it can take up to a year to determine the impact of food
sensitivities on patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) through a standard
elimination diet, since only one food group can be tested at a time. Improvements
to the standard elimination process of lifestyle interventions can provide
patients with effective, personalized treatment options more quickly.

Researchers at the University of California
Davis have developed an algorithmic lifestyle optimization (ALO) tool that analyzes
data from a group of patients to expedite the standard elimination approach and
quickly identify optimal lifestyle interventions. By utilizing a collection of
data that is influenced by multiple variables, it is possible to analyze a
variety of treatment options more quickly. After this data is collected, it then
undergoes iterative computations until an optimal treatment is discovered. The
ALO tool has shown promising results by creating dietary recommendations based
on realistic datasets. Using these datasets, it is estimated that ALO can
predict information about food sensitivities in patients with IBS around 60%
faster than testing with the standard elimination diet. The accuracy of the
standard elimination approach still applies, but conclusive results can be
found much more quickly by means of group testing. The time saved using this
approach can be beneficial in improving patients’ health and may allow personalized
medicine to become more accessible in the future.
applications:
-
Treatment of chronic medical conditions through personalized
lifestyle interventions.
-
Personalized diet and nutrition recommendations.
advantages:
-
More reliable than biomarker-based analysis in personalized
medicine.
-
Discovers optimal treatment options up to 60%
faster than standard elimination approach.
-
Supports personalized nutrition, wellness, and chronic
disease management strategies.

title: Isotryptamine Tetracycles for Treating Brain Disorders
meta_description: Researchers at the University of California, Davis have developed a technology for the treatment of neuropsychiatric and neurological diseases with compounds that enhance neural plasticity without the hallucinogenic effects.
summary:
Researchers at the University of California, Davis have
developed a technology for the treatment of neuropsychiatric and neurological
diseases with compounds that enhance neural plasticity without the
hallucinogenic effects.

This technology introduces novel
compounds, and their pharmaceutically acceptable salts, designed to increase
neural plasticity and dendritic spine density, thereby offering therapeutic
benefits for neuropsychiatric and neurological diseases. These compounds have
shown to rectify structural changes in the brain associated with such diseases,
including the loss of dendritic spines and synapses, while minimizing
hallucinogenic effects.
applications:

Pharmaceutical treatments for depression, anxiety,
addiction, and other neuropsychiatric disorders.
-
Therapeutic interventions for neurological
conditions with altered neural architecture.
-
Research tools in neurobiology and psychopharmacology.
advantages:
-
Enhances neural plasticity and dendritic spine density.
-
Non-hallucinogenic, making it suitable for a
broader patient population.
-
May treat a wide range of neuropsychiatric and
neurological diseases.
-
Improved physicochemical properties for better
clinical utility.
-
Potential for antidepressant, anxiolytic, and
anti-addictive effects.
-
Treats neuropsychiatric and neurological
diseases related to altered synaptic connectivity and plasticity.
-

background:
Telomeres are the end of eukaryotic chromosomes and shorten with time. Shortened telomeres cause disease in patients with short telomere syndromes. Cancer cells must activate telomerase to maintain telomeres to overcome senescence or apoptosis due to critically short

telomeres.

Telomere length is often measured by Southern Blot (invented in 1973). This method measures the length of all the telomeres in the cell and does not give quantitative information or information about individual telomere lengths. A quantitative PCR method was developed however it has many problems with reproducibility across different labs. The Single Telomere Length Analysis (STELA) method and the related Telomere Shortest Length Assay (TeSLA) targets individual telomeres, but the use of high cycles of PCR generates bias for shorter products.

Additionally, the use of Southern Blotting in STELA and TeSLA makes these techniques laborious and low-throughput. Currently, Telomere Flow FISH is the accepted clinical method for measuring telomere length. This method is highly reproducible, and can report on a specific cell type, however

it requires fresh blood samples and is not able to measure archival samples or tissues other than blood. The method uses an average of the telomeres without the ability to report the individual lengths of telomeres.

Thus, there are currently no methods that provide an accurate, high throughput, and simple approach for quantifying telomere length.
description:
Nobel Laureate Carol Greider and her team invented the TeloTag technique which enriches telomeric DNA for nanopore sequencing. This has allowed for exceedingly accurate determination of telomore length and composition.

The telomere tagging probe is ligated the telomere to generate a tagged telomere sequence and tagged telomere sequence is conjugated to a streptavidin functionalized via a biotin adapter on the tagged telomere sequence.

The bead is isolated and the tagged telomere sequence is recovered. The tagged telomere sequence can then by analyzed by any of a number of methods to determine the telomere length.

title:

Enhancing Lithium-Ion Battery Performance
meta_description: Researchers at the University of California, Santa Barbara introduce a novel multi-stage magnesiothermic reduction process that produces silicon oxide composites with smaller, more uniform silicon grains to improve lithium-ion battery anode performance. By limiting magnesium usage and distributing heat at each stage of the exothermic reaction, this method reduces the positive-feedback effect that typically causes uneven silicon grain sizes and formation of large silicon domains. The resulting nanosized, uniform silicon grains within the SiOx matrix demonstrate enhanced electrochemical properties including higher initial Coulombic efficiency, improved cycling stability, and better rate capability as lithium-ion battery anode materials. This approach also leverages low-cost borosilicate precursors to produce a novel electrode structure that avoids the need for carbon coatings, making it appealing for commercialization in the energy storage sector.
background: Silicon is one of the most promising anode materials to replace or complement the commercial graphite in lithium-ion batteries, due to its ten times the theoretical capacity of the graphite. The main challenges for silicon anodes are pulverization and instability of the solid-electrolyte interphase caused by the large volume change (∼300%) during cycling and undesirable side reactions between the active material and the electrolyte. Improving cycling stability is a key factor in silicon-based anode materials moving into the energy storage commercial market. It has been demonstrated that reducing the particle size to the nanoscale allows for silicon to withstand the (de)lithiation strains of the large volume change without fracture. However, nanosized silicon suffers from poor cycle life and low volumetric capacity density due to the unstable solid-electrolyte interphase and its low tap density.

summary: A pioneering framework that enables formal verification of Large Language Model (LLM) compliance with specified interaction protocols using natural language and Finite State Machine (FSM) structures. description:
This technology introduces a novel method to verify whether AI language models adhere to interaction rules. It is a comprehensive end-to-end framework that checks AI behavior against protocols written in natural language and structured using Finite State Machines (FSMs). The invention has three complementary components:

-
Core verification framework: Calibrates specification detail to match model capabilities, quantitatively measures protocol adherence, and supports certified deployment in safety-critical settings such as healthcare, finance, autonomous systems, and enterprise automation.
-
Rapid development module: A streamlined method for designing and iterating on protocols through efficient simulation. It enables faster protocol development than traditional approaches.
-

title: Targeted Nucleic Acid Editing via Cas9-Deaminase Fusion Proteins
meta_description: Traditional genome editing relying on double-stranded DNA breaks (DSBs) can cause unintended indels, translocation events, and cytotoxic responses in target cells. To overcome these limitations, a precise site-specific modification technology is required that operates without inducing double-stranded DNA cleavage. Developed by UC Berkeley researchers, this technology utilizes engineered fusion proteins comprising a Cas domain (such as a Cas9 nickase or dCas9) integrated with a nucleic acid-editing enzyme domain, such as a deaminase. The molecular mechanism leverages the RNA-guided targeted binding capability of Cas9 to localize the enzymatic editing domain to a specific genomic locus, facilitating direct nucleotide alterations (e.g., cytidine or adenosine conversions) without introducing double-stranded cuts. This system delivers high-precision target modification, significantly reduces off-target insertion/deletion mutations, and improves cell viability during genomic modifications compared to conventional double-strand cleavage mechanisms.

title: Process For Discovering Validating And Personalizing Transposable Cancer Vaccines
meta_description: Cancer inununotherapy heightens the immune system's ability to recognize a cancer and destroy the cancer cells, as opposed to more traditional compounds that directly inhibit the cancer's ability to proliferate. Cancer immunotherapy can provide good responses, even in advanced stages of cancer. Some current immunotherapies include cancer vaccines, antibodies, T cell infusions, and checkpoint blockade therapy. Malignant tumors often co-opt immune suppression and tolerance mechanisms to avoid immune destruction. Immune checkpoint blockade removes inhibitory signals of T-cell activation, which enables tumorreactive T cells to overcome regulatory mechanisms and mount an effective antitumor response. Accordingly, immune checkpoint blockade inhibits T cell-negative costimulation in order to unleash antitumor T-cell responses that recognize tumor antigens.However, only a subset of patients respond to current cancer immunotherapies, and it is difficult to predict which patients will respond. To increase the number of patients who benefit, combination therapies are being used. Cancer vaccine in combination with checkpoint blockade therapy is a promising approach to increasing the antitumor immune response. But, cancers typically have specific mutations (private mutations) in a person or individual tumor and cancer vaccines based on private mutations may be prohibitively expensive and inhibit widespread adoption of this approach.

Cancer inununotherapy heightens the immune system's ability to recognize a cancer and destroy the cancer cells, as opposed to more traditional compounds that directly inhibit the cancer's ability to proliferate. Cancer immunotherapy can provide good responses, even in advanced stages of cancer. Some current immunotherapies include cancer vaccines, antibodies, T cell infusions, and checkpoint blockade therapy. Malignant tumors often co-opt immune suppression and tolerance mechanisms to avoid immune destruction.

Immune checkpoint blockade removes inhibitory signals of T-cell activation, which enables tumorreactive T cells to overcome regulatory mechanisms and mount an effective antitumor response. Accordingly, immune checkpoint blockade inhibits T cell-negative costimulation in order to unleash antitumor T-cell responses that recognize tumor antigens.

However, only a subset of patients respond to current cancer immunotherapies, and it is difficult to predict which patients will respond. To increase the number of patients who benefit, combination therapies are being used. Cancer vaccine in combination with checkpoint blockade therapy is a promising approach to increasing the antitumor immune response. But, cancers typically have specific mutations (private mutations) in a person or individual tumor and cancer vaccines based on private mutations may be prohibitively expensive and inhibit widespread adoption of this approach.
description:
This technology involves the identification of personalized cancer vaccines that use public antigens that are shared across individuals. Genomewide

dysregulation of transcription and translation in cancer leads to overexpression of non-canonical protein coding genes, including transposable elements (TEs). TEs are strongly repressed in healthy cells to prevent genomic instability but can become dysregulated in cancer.

The technology further involves a computational framework for identifying potential cancer antigens within transposable elements, using e.g. RNA-seq, mass spectrometry, or other data. Some embodiments use autonomous transposable elements in the hmnan genome, e.g., L1HS.

Candidate cancer antigens are identified from expressed transposable elements. Differential expression levels are determined for proteins using baseline expression levels (using measurements of healthy tissue) and tumor expression levels (using measurements of tumor tissue). Protein(s) having a differential expression level greater than a threshold are selected.

Cancer vaccine(s) can then be generated for the selected cancer antigens. Particular cancer vaccines are selected for a patient based on differential expression levels for proteins using baseline expression levels of the patient and tumor expression levels of the patient. A vaccine for protein(s) having a differential expression level greater than a threshold can be selected.
applications:
Identification of potential tumor vaccine antigens, particularly those from transposable elements.

Identification of potential tumor vaccine antigens based on differential expression.

Generation of personalized tumor vaccines matched to, for example, MHC-I haplotype.
advantages: Makes use of overlooked cancer antigens such as transposable elements.

title: Dual Gasket System For Gas-Tight But Biocompatible Cell Culture Vessel Sealing
meta_description: Cell culture plates are an essential tool for cell biology research. They are used to grow cells in a controlled environment, which allows for study of the effects of different conditions on cell growth and development. The plates are typically made of plastic or glass and may have one or more wells, each of which can hold a small amount of cell culture media. The media provides the cells with the nutrients the cells need to grow and divide. Cell culture plates may be used in incubators to grow cells in a controlled environment. The incubator provides the cells with the necessary conditions for growth, including a constant temperature, humidity, and atmosphere.Conventional cell culture plates are susceptible to evaporation, which causes increased osmolarity of cell culture media. This in turn causes unrealistic growth of cells as well as potential differences between wells due to uneven evaporation. In addition, evaporation causes increased concentration of the salts involved in electrical signaling of electrically active cell types, changing the ionic gradients across the cell membrane, thereby affecting all characteristics of the initiation, transmission (and computation) in electrically active cells such as cardiac or neuronal cells.It is also difficult to maintain desired dissolved gas concentration with standard cell culture plates. This generally requires use of a compressed gas system, which uses gas regulators, sensors that are expensive and have limited lifetimes, and feedback control as well as a glove box for culture and/or handling.An incubator is used to maintain the desired temperature of the cell culture plates, but the incubator impedes access to the cultures for feeding, for microscopy, etc. Furthermore, observation equipment for use inside an incubator needs to be designed to resist incubator conditions (e.g., body temperature heat and humidity). Incubators also take up significant space and packing of incubators in a laboratory is space-inefficient relative to the form factor of the cell culture plates. As the number of cell culture plates in a single incubator increases, the ability of the incubator to perform its function decreases, since there is a minimum number of times an incubator may be accessed per week per cell culture vessel. background:
Cell culture plates are an essential tool for cell biology research. They are used to grow cells in a controlled environment, which allows for study of the effects of different conditions on cell growth and development. The plates are typically made of plastic or glass and may have one or more wells, each of which can hold a small amount of cell culture media. The media provides the cells with the nutrients the cells need to grow and divide. Cell culture plates may be used in incubators to grow cells in a controlled environment. The incubator provides the cells with the necessary conditions for growth, including a constant temperature, humidity, and atmosphere.

Conventional cell culture plates are susceptible to evaporation, which causes increased osmolarity of cell culture media. This in turn causes unrealistic growth of cells as well as potential differences between wells due to uneven evaporation. In addition, evaporation causes increased concentration of the salts involved in electrical signaling of electrically active cell types, changing the ionic gradients across the cell membrane, thereby affecting all characteristics of the initiation, transmission (and computation) in electrically active cells such as cardiac or neuronal cells.

It is also difficult to maintain desired dissolved gas concentration with standard cell culture plates. This generally requires use of a compressed gas system, which uses gas regulators, sensors that are expensive and have limited lifetimes, and feedback control as well as a glove box for culture and/or handling.

An incubator is used to maintain the desired temperature of the cell culture plates, but the incubator impedes access to the cultures for feeding, for microscopy, etc. Furthermore, observation equipment for use inside an incubator needs to be designed to resist incubator conditions (e.g., body temperature heat and humidity). Incubators also take up significant space and packing of incubators in a laboratory is space-inefficient relative to the form factor of the cell culture plates. As the number of cell culture plates in a single incubator increases, the ability of the incubator to perform its function decreases, since there is a minimum number of times an incubator may be accessed per week per cell culture vessel. However, every time the incubator is accessed, it is unable to perform its functions for a prolonged period of time, e.g., over 30 minutes.

A further technical problem is that cell culture devices that use an air gap for gas exchange have an increased risk of microbial contamination via that air gap. This makes it difficult to perform manual cell culture experiments over the course of months without contamination. In addition, cross-contamination is more likely if multiple different experiments are being performed in the same laboratory. Thus, there is a need for cell culture vessels and systems that overcome these problems.
description:
This is a mutli-material gasket construction which contains an inner cytocompatible gasket and outer gas impermeable gasket. It is to be used in cell culture vessels which require a wetted closure in which the closure must also be impermeable to carbon dioxide, oxygen and water vapor.

Sealing cell culture vessels using a closure where all of the wetted materials are compatible with cell culture, the closure is resistant to elevated pressures inside of the vessel and which does not allow carbon dioxide, oxygen or water vapor to leak in either direction across the closure.

This allows the interior of the cell culture vessel to have different oxygen and carbon dioxide concentrations from the outside. As well as being used for a closure in a cell culture vessel, this system may also be used elsewhere in a fluidic device for cell culture in order to hold a membrane in place in the case where this cannot be achieved using an adhesive or welding method (such as if the membrane needs to be replaceable.)

This device is used to create a gasketed seal between two rigid surfaces compressed together by some mechanism. The invention itself describes the design of the gasketing system

1) The inner gasket, in direct contact with the cell culture media, is made of fluorosilicone or silicone or another cell compatible elastomeric material.

2) The outer gasket, which surrounds the inner gasket and isolates it from the outside environment, is made of butyl rubber or a similar material which is relatively impermeable to oxygen, carbon dioxide and water vapor. This allows the use of an inner cell compatible gasket while also giving the closure the air impermeable properties of the outer gasket.

The cell culture vessel also includes a gas permeable film over the cell culture compartment. One side of the gas permeable film contacts cell culture media inside the cell culture compartment without an air gap in between.
applications:
Regulating gases (e.g., oxygen) and pH (via carbon dioxide) without any direct air contact with the cell culture media or air exchange with the outside environment.

The vessels use nonporous, gas permeable membranes to exchange gas with a regulating environment without water evaporation. These vessels are also totally sealed and do not require standard incubator equipment, making them compact and versatile devices for culturing cells, bacteria, etc.

Easier measurement and visualization of cells because analysis and imaging apparatus need not be placed inside the incubator.
advantages:
1) Closures sealed with gaskets made from cell culture compatible elastomeric materials such as silicone, (plasticized) fluorocarbon polymers such as FEP or plasticized PVDF or PVC are biocompatible but also extremely permeable to oxygen and carbon dioxide, making it difficult to maintain a different gas concentration inside and outside the vessel

2) Closures sealed with gaskets made from gas impermeable materials such as butyl rubber are not permeable to oxygen and carbon dioxide

3) Closures sealed with gaskets or mating surfaces made from slightly soft, biocompatible and gas impermeable materials such as PVDF or polypropylene require high closure forces and very uniform closure forces to make a seal which remains liquid-tight under pressure.

description: This is a design of microscope where the microscope (stage, lenses, lens barrel, optical filters, positioning apparatus) are designed to be used inside a cell culture incubator for imaging biological samples which need to be in an incubator for metabolic homeostasis and/or sterility reasons. Microscopes which fulfil this purpose of microscopy of living samples while they are being grown are called live-cell microscopes. In general, there are two existing designs of live cell microscope. The first are microscopes which are free-standing outside of an incubator and have a miniature incubator environment on the microscope stage and the microscope itself is outside the incubator. This constrains the microscope to samples of shapes and sizes acceptable to the miniature incubator environment and couples the biological homeostasis equipment to the microscope equipment. The second is a smaller microscope that is placed inside of an incubator in their entirety and include all of the optics, positioning apparatus and light sources for the microscope in a single monolithic unit which must all fit inside the cell culture incubator, often not leaving much space for anything else. This design is similar to the second approach, but is distinguished by having a light source separate from the rest of the microscope and coupled to one or more fiber optic cables. These fiber optics terminate in a detachable port attached to the optical apparatus of the in-incubator microscopes. The fiber optic cables may include light diffusers, collimators and, in the case of fluorescence microscopy, excitation filters. The light sources may be broad spectrum light sources for white light, reflected light or transillumination or they might be narrow spectrum light sources, such as fiber coupled LEDs or lasers which are used for excitation of fluorescent samples for fluorescence microscopy. For fluorescence microscopy, a broad spectrum light source with a bandpass filter may also be used. The fiber optic connection of the microscope is placed so as to illuminate the sample. This is via a part with a fiber optic port interposed in the microscope optical path such that the light emanating from the fiber illuminates the sample via epifluorescence using a dichroic mirror or beamsplitter. This part may allow automatic switching of a filter by having an inner component which holds multiple dichroic mirrors or beamsplitters at said angle and which can be positioned to place any of these optical elements in the path of the fiber optic illumination. The design places the light sources, which are bulky, heat producing and sensitive to their environment, outside of the incubator, where they are in a normal room environment, have access to cooling and are not subject to the space constraints of a cell culture incubator. The fiber coupled design of the microscope setup has the additional benefit that it renders the microscope setup modular and the light sources may be changed out between microscopes. Details ● Off the shelf components paired with laser cut sheet metal, which are all rated to survive indefinitely in an incubator ● Raspberry Pi HQ Camera, which uses a 12.3 megapixel Sony IMX477 sensor that captures images at up to 4056 x 3040 pixels ● Linear rail for motorized focus control ● Compatible with traditional microscope objectives ● Fluorescence excitation from Thorlabs LEDs with fiber optic cables ● Can be modified to incorporate 6 separate cameras instead of for six well cell culture plates ● 1 well version costs less than $2000
applications: Live cell microscopy
advantages: Unconstrained by in-incubator space requirements, allowing more space in-incubator for more samples or equipment or multiple microscopes. Harsh environment of the incubator does not effect the electronics of the light source. Limits the number of components which must be sanitized to be placed in the aseptic incubator environment. No need to account for the heat of a light source. Avoids costly and non-standard (with respect to lab power, alarm, gas source etc) microscope stage or in-microscope incubator solutions Can be used with any incubator. Allows sharing of light sources between microscopes.

background:
Expansion Reservoirs in Cell Culture Systems

Most cell culture systems incorporate an expansion reservoir to allow media exchange - the removal and replacement of culture media—without drying out the cells.

This function is implemented in various ways, depending on the system design:

Conventional culture systems (e.g., wells, flasks, and basic bioreactors) use the culture chamber itself as an expansion reservoir. These chambers hold excess liquid media, which can be gradually removed and replaced. As liquid volume changes, it is balanced by air entering or exiting the chamber.

Circulating fluidic systems (e.g., perfusion bioreactors) typically include a dedicated inline expansion reservoir. In these systems, part of the media is actively circulated through the system (“circulation pathway”), while another part remains static in the reservoir. Media is exchanged from the non-circulating volume, with air compensating for the volume change.

Flexible bag systems and air-free flexible chamber systems (including recirculating setups) also support media exchange, but instead of displacing air, the flexible container itself changes shape to accommodate volume changes.

Despite their differences, all of these systems share key characteristics:

- They support variable liquid volumes during media exchange.

- They require separate actuators (e.g., pumps or valves) for draining and refilling media.

We define all these systems as cell culture systems that rely on an expansion reservoir.

Challenges of Expansion Reservoir-Based Systems

Mechanical and Control Complexity:

- Using separate mechanisms for draining and refilling media increases system complexity - Multiple actuators must be precisely controlled and synchronized, which introduces more potential points of failure.

Media Dilution and Wastage :

- To avoid drying out the sample, the system must hold both: - A minimum media volume to support the biological sample - Additional dead volume (e.g., in pumps, sensors, and tubing) that must remain wetted - In systems with large dead volumes, this can exceed the minimum required for biological homeostasis, leading to dilution of both: - Endogenous substances (e.g., signaling molecules, hormones, biomarkers), which may affect cell behavior or impair data accuracy - Exogenous additives (e.g., nutrients, growth factors), which are costly and may be wasted. Reduced Sensitivity of Analytical Measurements: - Diluted media lowers the concentration of analytes (e.g., metabolic byproducts, gene expression markers), reducing the sensitivity of diagnostic readouts. If some old media remains in the system during exchange, it may delay detection of biological changes. Physical Bulk and System Complexity - Expansion reservoirs add to both the physical size and operational complexity of the apparatus, which can reduce efficiency, increase cost, and complicate system management. Air-Related Issues - In systems where liquid volume is balanced by air volume, air introduces several risks: - Air bubble formation (e.g., from surface exposure or in expansion tanks) can: - Disturb gas concentrations - Cause local precipitation or concentration of solutes - Physically disrupt cells, sensors, or fluid flow (e.g., by turbulence, blockage, or altered mixing). - Evaporation and osmotic imbalance occur when: - Air space humidity is insufficient to prevent evaporation or airflow is great enough to cause loss through advection - Temperature or pressure changes affect relative humidity or gas solubility. - Gas concentration control is difficult: - It either requires active feedback with gas lines and actuators to manage air composition in the dead space, or - Continuous air replacement, which increases complexity and promotes further evaporation through water vapor loss due to advection. Other physical parameters that expansion reservoir based systems struggle to control:

Fluid Pressure:

- Having an expansion reservoir, which inherently involves equilibration of the internal pressure of a system with some surrounding environment makes it impossible to maintain the fluid pressure of the entire media compartment of a cell culture system at a pressure other than that of the expansion reservoir. - Therefore, to achieve fluidic pressures other than this expansion reservoir pressure, more complicated methods of establishing fluid pressure must be used, such as ones which use active pumping and fluidic resistors or that require repletion of a gravity-pressurized reservoir. - In fluid systems, achieving elevated or reduced pressures is crucial for controlling the flow and behavior of fluids within a model, especially when working with fluidic resistors and circulation pumps. Fluidic resistors are components that impede the flow of fluid, and by varying the resistance, they help regulate pressure within a system. - When paired with circulation pumps, they provide a dynamic way to maintain or adjust pressure levels. However, using this setup introduces complexity in pressure control. To achieve and maintain the desired - pressure, a pressure feedback control system becomes essential. - This system monitors the pressure within the circuit and adjusts the pump's speed or resistance in real time to ensure the pressure stays within the desired range. - Without this feedback loop, fluctuations in pressure could lead to inefficiencies or system malfunctions. - Pressure feedback control itself adds complexity because it often requires sophisticated sensors, controllers, and algorithms to keep the pressure stable. - These systems need to react quickly to changes in fluid dynamics, such as those caused by variations in fluid temperature, viscosity or flow rate. - Moreover, the system must be calibrated to handle different conditions, such as varying load demands or system wear over time. - Additionally, there is the risk of overpressure, which can occur if the pressure exceeds safe operating limits. - In such cases, components like pressure relief valves or bypass lines become critical. - Pressure relief valves open when pressure exceeds a certain threshold, allowing excess fluid to be diverted to prevent damage to the system. - Bypass lines, on the other hand, allow fluid to flow around the system or around particular components to relieve pressure buildup. - Both overpressure relief mechanisms add extra layers of complexity to the design and operation of the system. They must be carefully designed and sized to ensure proper operation under all possible conditions. - Without them, there's a significant risk of damaging pumps, resistors, or other sensitive components due to excessive pressure, which could lead to system failure or safety hazards. - Elevated or reduced pressures can be achieved in models containing fluidic resistors paired with circulation pumps - however these require added complexity in pressure feedback control and may require additional complexity in overpressure relief and/or bypass line components to avoid damaging overpressure events. - In a more complex design for expansion reservoirs, elevated or reduced pressures can be achieved in models containing an airliquid interface by simultaneous pressurization/depressurization of the air compartment as well as the liquid compartment, however this alters the relationship between gas partial pressure and gas molar concentration, requiring added complexity in gas provision feedback control - The difficulty of these approaches is problematic because certain biological processes and tissues require specific pressure conditions that are not at ambient levels, and if these pressure conditions can't be modeled accurately, it is difficult to simulate real-life conditions of certain organ tissues. - Some tissues experience pulsatile (regularly changing or "pumping") pressures, such as blood flow through arteries, or even pressure that changes dynamically over time due to body processes. - These fluctuating pressures are important for mimicking real physiological conditions. Vascularized tissues (tissues with bloo vessels) rely on pressure gradients (differences in pressure) to function correctly. For example, blood pressure helps circulate nutrients and oxygen throughout tissues.
description:
In its simplest form, the system comprises

- A cell culture fluid recirculation loop which has a fixed fluidic volume or at least an upper bound on said volume. - A controllable recirculation pump. - A controllable pump on an inflow line which may inject fresh media into the recirculation loop, combined with either a one-way valve, or a pump design which does not allow for backflow, to keep media contained at the injection port. - A normally closed outflow valve on an outflow line which either is passively opened at a defined cracking pressure, or an actively controllable valve which can be selectively opened - thereby acting as a one-way valve which is only opened during media change. - This keeps media contained within the circulation loop as to not exit via the outflow line when media change is not being effected. - The media change pump injects into the recirculation loop via a T junction - The outflow line ejects from the recirculation loop via a T junction - With respect to the culture well or the component of the circulation loop with the largest volume, the injection line should join the loop upstream and the ejection line should leave the loop downstream, relative to the normal direction of circulation, such that a media change effected by the media change pump will be capable of ejecting the largest possible volume of media contained between the two points. - Media change is effected by injecting media via the controllable fresh media injection pump. This can be done with the recirculation pump either circulating or not circulating. Since the recirculation loop has a fixed or upper bounded volume, injection of fluid will cause an excess of volume to enter the loop - requiring that, as a consequence of the outflow valve opening at a fixed or upper bounded fluidic pressure, liquid will be ejected from the loop to equalize pressure. - This pressure regulation by fluid ejection can be effected either by a passive valve which opens at a certain pressure or by an actively controlled valve with feedback control on pressure - Specifically, this media change occurs via continuous displacement and ejection of fluid from inside the loop by new fluid entering the loop. The fluid volume contained in the loop will remain the same during the media change. - This is in contrast to traditional methods of media exchange where media is removed from and added to the loop sequentially, altering the fluid volume of the loop during the media change. - Optionally, there may be an occlusive valve in the fluidic loop which redirects fluid out of the outflow port and prevents recirculation. This will allow the pump apparatus to replace fluid in the loop with a minimum of mixing. - This valve might be a second role played by the recirculation pump itself, if the pump is of an occlusive design such as a peristaltic pump. - Optionally, to perform gas exchange without needing a reservoir or open component containing an air volume, the system may contain a mechanism for gas exchange which may be permeable tubing (eg silicone, plasticised PVC) a hollow-fiber gas exchanger, a silicone or permeable plastic chamber or a membrane gas exchanger. - This gas exchanger should have a fixed internal fluid volume - Optionally, the system may contain a fluidic damper, a waveform generator, a pressure-generating accessory such as a syringe pump or other device to alter the pressure dynamically or statically, - so long as these devices have a bounded internal fluid volume and/or can have their fluid volume restricted during a media change. - Optionally, one or more of the inflow or outflow pumps may be used to dynamically or statically alter the pressure in the system separate from media change by addition or removal of fluid. - Optionally, the system may contain multiple wells, in parallel or in series within the fluidic loop. - Optionally, the system may consist of parallel replicates who share the same inflow or outflow pump actuators but which are fluidically isolated within their circuits.
applications:
Cell culture systems

Bioreactor systems
advantages:
1) In this fixed/bounded volume system, injection of a fluid bolus is all that is needed to effect a media change. A media change can occur in a single action, with simultaneous injection and ejection of media and unchanging fluid volume.

a. In other systems, such as those with fluid expansion tanks, those with open wells, those with robotized pipetting, separate media removal and media addition effectors (pumps, pipettes, etc) must operate sequentially to effect a media change.

b. In more complex systems, such as those with fluid expansion tanks or open wells, the approach is different. These systems often involve a separate sequential media removal and media addition process.

i. For example, in a system with a fluid expansion tank, you may need to first remove the old media (through a pump or pipette) before adding the new media.

ii. This ensures the system is emptied before the new media is introduced.

iii. In robotized pipetting systems, automated processes use pipettes or other robotic tools to carefully withdraw and dispense fluids. The addition and removal are performed one after the other, which can take longer but ensures precise control over the volumes involved.

2) The boundary layer of the fluid is not displaced during a media change because the volume of fluid does not change.

a. This avoids disturbing structures inside the bioreactor by changing the fluid boundary.

b. This avoids the possibility of drying out any sample within the device. This is a large problem in open welled microfluidic devices. c. This eliminates the possibility of underfilling or overfilling a well due to inaccuracy in pumps causing an imbalance between media addition and media extraction. d. Any media change mechanism which involves sequentially removing and filling media from a well, or vice versa will alter the fluid boundary.

3) Since media change is performed by a single action and does not involve the coordination of multiple pumps, and because the fluid volume is fixed, it is possible to simultaneously perfuse and media change in the system without having to halt the normal operation of the bioreactor.

a. This is important for samples which depend on consistent physical cues.

b. Media change can be performed while maintaining a fixed perfusion rate equal to the rate when not media changing.

c. Media change can also be done in a continuous “trickle” fashion, eliminating the discrete media change intervals causing abrupt alterations in chemical environment seen in conventional cell culture.

4) Since the system is entirely closed and is completely filled, without any air liquid interface which might change based on the strength or direction of gravitational force, the apparatus can be used without restrictions or alterations to design in non-stationary formats.

a. The system to effect a complete media change without removal from a shaker, or from a rotating or rolling bioreactor apparatus.

b. This allows the system to be used in zero gravity.

5) Comparison to other closed perfusion bioreactors and closed bag culture systems:

a. Systems already exist which have the benefits of not having an air boundary, eliminating issues with air contact, but they still contain expansion reservoirs, adding complexity to media changes and making pressure control difficult.

b. The NASA Bioculture system also employs a closed perfusion bioreactor system with no air in the loop.

i. However, they use an inline reservoir with a deformable wall and variable volume, such that separate media injection and ejection steps are required to change media:

ii. there is an expansion reservoir, just sealed by a flexible skin.

iii. the deformable reservoir means that fluid pressure cannot remain fixed especially during the media change, because the deformable wall equalizes pressure with the environment.

iv. having a reservoir increases the fluid volume of the system, which causes dilution of added substances (wasting reagents) and dilution of circulating biological factors (altering biochemistry and diluting measurable biomarkers.)

c. Cell expansion systems such as the Xuri Cell Expansion System or Sartorius RM bioreactors use a sealed bioreactor which may be operated without an air-liquid interface and which may be run in perfusion or recirculatory perfusion,

i. but they employ fluid reservoirs which have deformable walls and do not possess minimum interior filled volumes.

ii. This has two consequences:

1. first, separate, sequential fluid addition and fluid removal mechanisms are required and second,

2. the internal pressure of the fluid may equalize with the surrounding ambient pressure.

background:
Problem 1: In conventional static or rocking 3D culture systems, nutrients and oxygen reach cells mainly by diffusion, which is too slow to penetrate thick tissues (>200 μm). This leads to necrotic cores and poor viability or maturation. By generating a controlled pressure gradient across the tissue, the invention drives convective perfusion (bulk flow) through the tissue block or hydrogel. This allows continuous exchange of nutrients, gases, and signaling molecules deep inside, extending viable tissue thickness and lifespan.

Problem 2: In certain tissues, fluidic cues also shape tissue organization and function. Most organoid or 3D culture systems lack physiologically relevant interstitial flow, an important mechanical cue for morphogenesis, endothelial alignment, and extracellular matrix remodeling. The pressure-driven perfusion creates interstitial shear forces and gradients similar to those in living tissues, improving differentiation and structural organization.

Problem 3: Many bioreactors rely on imprecise or uncontrolled flow rates and pressures that do not guarantee a stable or known pressure difference across the tissue. For example, gravity fed microfluidic apparatuses which generate pressure differentials have their pressure gradient constantly changing because the difference in fluidic column height changes as the fluid equilibrates. Rocker based "perfusion" systems have a similar problem because rocking is inherently oscillatory and causes the involved forces to be constantly changing.

Problem 4: Capillary to tissue pressure gradients in vivo are on the order of 10-15 mmHg. This is 10 or more times higher than generated by gravity fed or rocker perfusion systems. We anticipate needing a larger pressure gradient for perfusion in thicker tissues as well, since we seek to perfuse tissues much thicker than normal intercapillary distances. In our system, we have successfully generated gradients as high as 200 mmHg (limited by tissue integrity, not by our fluidic actuators.)

Problem 5: Surgical specimens or organ slices can’t easily be perfused with microfluidic chips, which are typically designed for engineered scaffolds. By using two fluidic compartments sandwiching any tissue-containing block or hydrogel, the system can adapt to irregular natural tissue samples, not just engineered constructs.

Problem 6: Self-contained culture systems with pressure gradient generation within a closed device (such as gravity and rocker devices) often make it difficult to monitor metabolites, oxygen, or pH dynamically. Because fluid continuously circulates through defined compartments, it can integrate inline sensors (e.g., pressure, oxygen, conductivity, FTIR) for real-time monitoring and feedback control.

Problem 7: Traditional perfusion systems often require high media volumes or continuous replacement, increasing reagent costs and diluting secreted factors of interest. This design allows for a closed fluidic loop circulation system minimizes media consumption while maintaining exchange efficiency. The ability to adjust flow and pressure allows optimization for either steady-state homeostasis or accumulation of secreted products.
description:
Perfusion of a semi-permeable tissue-containing block by means of a pressure gradient in a circulatory bioreactor

This invention is the method of using a bioreactor which has two media filled fluidic compartments separated by a block of tissue (e.g. flattened organoid, 3D layered cells, surgical specimen) or a hydrogel which contains tissue. The two media filled compartments have circulating media flowing through them, supplied by a fluidic apparatus which circulates fluid using a pump. In one case, the two compartments are in series with respect to fluid circulation, and a variable orifice valve (e.g. an IV stopcock, needle valve or ball valve) is placed in between the two, such that an elevated pressure is generated in the upstream compartment relative to the downstream compartment, establishing a pressure gradient across the tissue containing block.

In a secondary aspect, the two compartments are in parallel, and a shunting pump from the low pressure compartment to the high pressure compartment generates the pressure gradient. In both cases, the outcome is to generate a pressure gradient from one side of the tissue containing block to the other, providing a motivating force for perfusion through the tissue containing block.

Our invention relates to methods, devices, and compositions for generating a controlled pressure gradient across a tissue-containing block, thereby enabling convective perfusion through three-dimensional biological tissues, organoids, or tissue-mimetic hydrogels. The invention provides a compact, sealed, and tunable bioreactor system capable of maintaining physiologically relevant flow and pressure conditions without requiring an external incubator or complex pneumatic equipment.

In one embodiment, the invention provides a bioreactor apparatus comprising two media-filled fluidic compartments separated by a tissue-containing block. The tissue-containing block may include a biological specimen such as a flattened organoid, multicellular layer, hydrogel embedded with cells, or excised tissue sample. The block serves as a semipermeable barrier between the compartments, allowing media to flow through interstitial spaces, hydrogel pores or engineered or grown capillary blood vessels while maintaining structural separation. The compartments are fluidically connected to one another and to a circulation circuit containing at least one pump configured to drive liquid media flow.

The system is sealed from the external environment to preserve aseptic conditions and to permit buildup of hydrostatic pressure. In a series-flow configuration, the upstream and downstream compartments are arranged sequentially in the circulation loop. The outlet of the upstream compartment is connected to the inlet of the downstream compartment through a variable orifice valve such as a stopcock, needle valve, or microfluidic constriction. Operation of the pump generates circulation of the culture medium through the system, and adjustment of the variable orifice produces a controlled pressure drop across the valve. This in turn elevates the pressure in the upstream compartment relative to the downstream compartment, thereby generating a defined pressure gradient across the tissue-containing block.

The magnitude of the gradient can be tuned by adjusting pump speed or valve resistance, permitting physiological interstitial pressures to be established across the tissue. In an alternative parallel-flow configuration, the two compartments are positioned in separate but fluidically linked loops, each receiving medium from a common pump or reservoir. A shunting pump or equivalent pressure-elevating mechanism transfers fluid from the downstream (low-pressure) compartment back to the upstream (high-pressure) compartment. The rate of this shunting flow defines the steady-state pressure differential between compartments, which again results in a trans-tissue pressure gradient across the tissue-containing block. This configuration enables independent control of the pressure and flow rate within each compartment and may be advantageous for maintaining asymmetric or bidirectional perfusion conditions.

The system includes pressure and flow sensors placed upstream and downstream of the tissue block to measure and regulate the pressure differential. Data from these sensors can be used for closed-loop feedback control of the pump or valve, ensuring constant perfusion parameters over extended periods. The entire fluidic circuit may be constructed from biocompatible, sterilizable materials such as polycarbonate, glass, silicone, or polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE). Tubing may include sterile sampling ports. The medium may be oxygenated by a gas-permeable membrane module, maintained in an incubator using an open reservoir or gas permeable tubing or maintained under sealed, pre-equilibrated conditions.

In preferred embodiments, the system is operated as a closed-loop recirculatory circuit, allowing long-term culture without manual media exchanges. The sealed design maintains sterility and also enables safe containment of hazardous, infectious, or genetically modified biological materials. Because gas exchange, temperature regulation, and perfusion are maintained internally, the device can operate independently of an external incubator, providing a portable and self-contained culture environment.

The tissue-containing block positioned between the two fluidic compartments may include a natural or synthetic hydrogel, a decellularized tissue scaffold, or an intact tissue slice. In some embodiments, the tissue block comprises a composite of biological tissue and hydrogel matrix. The matrix composition is selected to provide permeability suitable for interstitial flow under modest pressure differentials. The matrix stiffness and porosity are tuned to resist compression under flow while maintaining structural integrity and viable cellular microenvironments. The block may be held in place by a compressible gasket, porous support ring (eg a porous PTFE or glass filter element on a support), or clamping frame that seals the perimeter while allowing flow through the interior volume.

The invention further encompasses a method of using the described bioreactor to perfuse biological tissues. The method includes the steps of (a) positioning a tissue-containing block between two fluidic compartments, (b) filling the compartments with liquid culture medium, (c) circulating the medium through the compartments using a pump, and (d) establishing a controllable pressure differential between the compartments using a flow restriction or shunting pump. The pressure gradient thus produced drives interstitial perfusion through the tissue-containing block, resulting in improved oxygenation, nutrient delivery, waste removal, and mechanical stimulation. The method may include monitoring the pressure differential and adjusting flow parameters to maintain physiological interstitial flow conditions.

The method can be applied to organoid cultures, engineered tissues, or explanted specimens for purposes including long-term culture, drug screening, toxicology testing, and disease modeling. In some embodiments, the invention further includes a tissue-hydrogel composite composition specifically designed for use in the described pressure-gradient bioreactor. The composition comprises a biological component, such as living cells or tissue fragments, dispersed within a porous, biocompatible hydrogel matrix. The composite exhibits sufficient permeability to permit interstitial flow and sufficient mechanical stability to withstand pressure-driven perfusion without deformation. The material properties of the composite, including porosity, compressive modulus, and permeability, are selected to yield stable convective flow and oxygen transport at physiologically relevant pressures. The composite may also incorporate biomolecular gradients, embedded sensors, or structural reinforcements to enhance reproducibility and analytical performance.

Collectively, the above-described features produce several synergistic advantages. The application of a controlled pressure gradient across the tissue-containing block overcomes diffusion limitations that restrict the thickness of viable 3D tissues in static culture, while reproducing the interstitial flow and mechanical cues found in vivo. The sealed recirculatory design reduces contamination risk and simplifies aseptic maintenance. The incorporation of standard valves, tubing, and pumps minimizes fabrication complexity and cost, enabling broad adoption. The system can be scaled from single-unit benchtop reactors to multiplexed arrays for high-throughput experiments.

The invention provides a novel combination of structural and functional elements—a dual-compartment bioreactor, a pressure-modulating fluidic circuit, and a perfusable tissue composition—that together enable controlled, sterile, and physiologically relevant perfusion of three-dimensional biological tissues. This configuration allows precise generation of interstitial pressure gradients through natural or engineered tissue blocks, achieving improved viability, biological realism, and experimental accessibility relative to existing culture systems.

advantages:
WO2022226405A1 - "Fluidic platforms for perfusable vascular tissues" includes an embodiment involving a microfluidic chip which contains a tissue containing block separating two perfusable fluidic compartments, but uses gravity columns to provide pressure. This does not allow integration into a circulating culture loop. This does not allow for dynamic (e.g. computer driven actuator) control over pressure gradients. This does not allow for a stable pressure gradient due to changes in the gravity column heights. This does not allow for physiological pressure gradients, since a constant column height in excess of 10cm would be needed.

US11680241B2 - "Perfusion enabled bioreactors", in its main design, also uses a gravity column to force fluid through a tissue containing block in a similar way to WO2022226405A1. It has two additional methods of providing a pressure gradient, one of which is to attach the outflow to a vacuum line, and the other is to use a screw mechanism on a lid to distract the lid, causing a relative vacuum. This device integrates sealed, noncirculating fluidic chambers into the device, where either a gravity column difference or applied vacuum provides pressure gradient, and this design prevents media changes without having to disassemble portions of the device. Without vacuum, a constant column height in excess of 10cm would be needed, which is not provided for in the design. With vacuum, access to the culture device is impeded, furthermore, failure to cease vacuum before all media has been pulled through the device would lead to a catastrophic failure through aspiration of air through the sample.

https://doi.org/10.3390/bioengineering11111147 - "An Arteriovenous Bioreactor Perfusion System for Physiological In Vitro Culture of Complex Vascularized Tissue Constructs" describes a similar two-compartment system with circulatory flow however, it requires separate arterial and venous pressure control, increasing system complexity.

https://research.utoronto.ca/technology-opportunities/db/microfluidic-device-and-pump-system-vascularization-organoids "Microfluidic Device and Pump System for Vascularization of Organoids" has a similar arterio-venous design, but is a monolithic miniature microfluidic chip, where there is no ability to manipulate the fluidic resistance, and the mixed nonocclusive impeller design and fixed resistance would struggle to generate physiological pressure gradients. Furthermore, this depends on the use of an incubator, which ours does not.

Within our group, we have also created a version of this where there is no circulation outflow of the chamber on either side, therefore making it difficult to control pressure gradient -- small changes in actuator force can cause large changes in compartment pressure on either side, without a recourse for outflow of fluid. Overpressure events thereby often rupture the intervening tissue containing block. We note that US11680241B2 likely has this same problem for the same reason, though it is not discussed.

title: Power-Efficient Coherent Optical Transceiver for Data Centers
meta_description: Researchers at the University of California, Santa Barbara have developed a scalable optoelectronic transceiver that combines tunable traveling-wave modulation and analog coherent reception to support power-efficient, high-speed optical links. This technology integrates traveling-wave Mach-Zehnder modulators, driver biasing, optical amplification, and wavelength and polarization multiplexing with analog coherent receivers. The receiver separates polarization channels and uses local-oscillator detection and feedback-based control to recover transmitted signals, supporting wavelength-multiplexed communication for data-center networks.Patent application: https://patents.google.com/patent/US20240089001A1/enPublication: https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/9606026
background: Intra-datacenter traffic has increased significantly in the past few years, placing increasingly stringent cost and power consumption requirements on optical transceivers. As both the start and end point in fiber-optic communications, optoelectronic transceivers have the potential to increase the efficiency of fiber-optic communications; however, current optoelectronic transmitters have limitations imposed by fabrication. Many optoelectronic transmitters are fabricated based on narrow-band ring-resonator modulators, which can be very sensitive to process and temperature variations compared to Mach-Zehnder modulators (MZMs). There is a need for optical transceivers that are power-efficient and can provide high-speed data transfer over long distances.

title: Sealed Chamber For Cmos-Mea
meta_description: Technical Problem1. Evaporation and Osmolarity Shifts: In open-well culture systems and vapor permeable closed systems, media evaporation causes osmotic toxicity especially during long-term electrophysiology experiments that can last days or weeks. Even inside a highly humidified incubator significant evaporation occurs over time. This alters the osmolarity of the cell culture medium, increases salt concentrations and affects electrophysiology, which in cells are driven by ionic gradients. By creating a hermetic, non-evaporative liquid seal, this invention completely halts evaporation and maintains a stable osmotic environment. 2. Contamination and Environmental Cross-Talk: Open designs leave cultures vulnerable to airborne particulate, bacterial or fungal contamination, especially during transport or when handled outside a sterile hood for imaging or electrical recording. The sealed well insert physically isolates the biological sample, protecting it from external contaminants and preventing cross-talk between separate wells. This is important especially when combined with electrophysiology equipment which cannot fully or easily be sterilized due to complex and sensitive electronics.3. Incompatibility of Closed-System Benefits with Legacy Hardware: Researchers looking for closed, tightly controlled fluidic environments have traditionally been forced to abandon standard commercial CMOS-MEA platforms in favor of bespoke microfluidic chips and bespoke electrode arrays. This invention solves this compatibility barrier by offering a retrofit mechanism. Clamping or gluing a base to the exterior of existing, commercially available well and adding sealing to this allows full use of sophisticated commercial equipment.4. This insert eliminates the direct air gap above the cell culture media. Removing this interface completely prevents the water evaporation and subsequent boundary-layer shifts that typically degrade long-term cultures.5. Traditional MEAs must sit inside bulky, expensive incubators to maintain gas and temperature stability. This invention inherits the self-contained environmental isolation of the prior patent. Because gas and fluid exchange are handled through dedicated routing within the closed well, the MEA device can function reliably on a benchtop, inside a microscope chamber or in specialized testing setups without losing environmental control.6. Precise, Multi-Gas and pH Equilibrium: The architecture leverages the closed-system mechanics of the prior application to maintain strict carbon dioxide, oxygen and carbonic acid equilibrium. It allows researchers to introduce targeted gas-controlled fluids or direct gas feeds to regulate pH and oxygen levels precisely at the sensor surface, achieving localized environmental profiles (such as deep hypoxia) that are impossible to maintain in an open petri dish structure.

description:
Method of transforming commercial CMOS-MEA wells or other petri dish-type wells into sealed fluidic chambers for incubator-free sealed cell culture

This invention is a specialized insert designed for commercial CMOS-MEA wells that adapts the closed, non-evaporative cell culture technology of patent application WO2025024652A1 to petri-dish-like well structures. The apparatus operates by securing a base to the exterior of the well via clamping or gluing, using a mechanical screw or clamp mechanism to tightly compress the well insert against the base. Using with gas-impermeable and biocompatible gaskets, this architecture establishes a completely isolated fluidic environment that prevents liquid or gas ingress and egress. Integrated ports in the lid enable precise fluid ingress, air evacuation, continuous liquid flow and the targeted introduction of compounds to modulate cellular electrical activity.

Key Components of the Device:

The device assembly consists of an external mounting collar designed to couple mechanically to the outer perimeter of the pre-existing, rigid plastic or ceramic well housing of the CMOS-MEA. By anchoring exclusively to this exterior structure, the collar establishes a mechanical load path that completely bypasses the delicate internal silicon sensor matrix. Within this collar sits the fluidic well insert manifold, which is fabricated as a rigid plug that fits precisely inside the internal well diameter. This manifold contains internal fluidic routing channels terminating in external fluidic interfaces such as tapered hose barbs or female Luer lock connectors. It may also feature an integrated, rigid mechanical stop collar engineered to establish an absolute axial displacement limit during assembly.

Axial force is applied through an axial compression mechanism, which can be configured either as an internally threaded, free-spinning outer sleeve that engages the external mounting collar or as a circumferential array of peripheral bolts. This mechanism transforms rotational force into uniform downward linear displacement without imparting torsional shear to the underlying seals. The sealing interface itself relies on a dual-concentric elastomeric gasket system situated on the lower face of the insert manifold. If gas impermeability is not needed, or a material with sufficient gas barrier function as well as biocompatibility is chosen, then only one gasket is needed.

These gaskets include an inner ring and an outer ring positioned in close proximity, which work together to form a redundant hermetic barrier against the internal well wall. The operational method establishes a controlled, non-evaporative fluidic environment through a precise sequence of mechanical and hydraulic steps. First, the external mounting collar is rigidly secured to the outer perimeter of the CMOS-MEA well ring using a structural adhesive or a high-friction mechanical clamp. Once this base is secure, the fluidic well insert manifold, pre-fitted with the gasket(s), is aligned and lowered into the internal cavity of the CMOS-MEA well.

Next, the axial compression mechanism is engaged and driven downward using a torque-limiting instrument, such as a calibrated torque screwdriver or torque wrench. This instrument rotates the threaded sleeve or the peripheral bolting array until the integrated stop collar seats firmly against the mounting collar. This action achieves a precise, reproducible percentage of elastomeric deflection across both gaskets without overloading the underlying chip architecture. Finally, fluid is injected under positive pressure through the designated ingress port, forcing the gas phase out through the egress port as the liquid front rises. This process continues until the entire internal headspace is occupied by liquid, which effectively eliminates the gas-liquid interface.

By combining the external mounting base with a rigid well insert and dedicated fluidic ports, this device converts a standard open-top electrophysiology well into a completely closed microfluidic chamber. This mechanical arrangement allows the fluidic and thermodynamic principles of the parent patent to be applied directly to commercial MEA hardware. The hydraulic method of filling the well through these ports completely eliminates the gas-liquid interface right above the sensor matrix. This directly replicates the non-evaporative environment of the parent patent, stopping media evaporation and stabilizing osmolarity over long-term recordings without needing complex incubation infrastructure.

The entirely fluid filled well and gasketed sealing enables this closed-system isolation to function in a live electrophysiology context. This sealing means thqat the well remains entirely isolated from atmospheric gas fluctuations while maintaining a safe envirornment for the cells. This complete isolation also allows for precise localized control over gas concentrations and compound delivery directly at the sensor surface. Consequently, researchers can achieve the exact environmental stability and precise chemical modulation described in the previously filed patent application using existing electrophysiology well designs.

applications: CMOS-MEA analysis of organoids - particularly brain organoids.
advantages:
Existing attempts to manage the environment in CMOS-MEA wells include commercial perfusion lids provided by equipment manufacturers or custom-built lids developed by academic laboratories. These systems typically maintain an atmospheric air gap above the cell culture media and rely on external incubator infrastructure to balance temperature and gas concentrations. The current invention differs by eliminating the gas-liquid interface entirely through a hermetic seal. By avoiding the air gap, it stops evaporation at the root and operates stably without specialized incubation enclosures.

Another approach involves using gas-permeable film lids stretched over the top of the culture wells. While these films allow gas exchange and attempt to restrict evaporation, they introduce new technical challenges. Water vapor still escapes through the film over extended periods, which gradually alters media osmolarity during long-term experiments. Furthermore, the temperature differential between the warm media and the cooler film lid causes significant condensation to form on the underside of the film. This condensation can drop back into the well, disrupting the local environment, or it can obscure optical imaging. This invention solves these issues by using a rigid well insert with gas-impermeable gaskets that completely seals the chamber. Since there is no air layer, there is no evaporation and condensation within the well.

Researchers who require strict fluidic isolation and automated drug delivery often turn to custom microfluidic or organ-on-a-chip platforms, usually fabricated from PDMS or injection-molded plastics. While these platforms achieve excellent environmental control, they are incompatible with high-density commercial CMOS-MEA hardware. Choosing these custom systems forces researchers to abandon market-standard recording consoles, losing access to high-resolution electrical stimulation and sub-cellular recording capabilities. This invention acts as a bridge by providing a retrofittable microfluidic environment that clamps directly onto existing commercial well structures, allowing users to keep their high-density sensor infrastructure while gaining the benefits of a closed fluidic circuit.

In comparison to the previously filed WO2025024652A1: The previous patent application describes a standalone closed-system cell culture vessel that eliminates the air gap using a gas-permeable, liquid-impermeable film. However, that design cannot be applied directly to commercial CMOS-MEA chips, which feature rigid plastic or ceramic well walls permanently bonded around a highly fragile silicon sensor. Attempting to press a simple film or standard lid onto these pre-existing commercial well rims leads to uneven sealing, fluid leakage or structural damage to the underlying electronic array. This invention improves upon the design in WO2025024652A1 by introducing a multi-part mechanical assembly. By clamping a dedicated base to the exterior of the commercial well ring and using a separate screw or clamp mechanism to compress the gasketed insert downward, the sealing forces are safely distributed away from the delicate sensor surface. This mechanical adaptation allows the closed, non-evaporative fluidic principles of the parent patent to be safely retrofitted onto standard commercial hardware.
